name: Impressions and ideas
plain_explanation: Hume divides all mental contents ('perceptions') into two kinds: 'impressions,' the vivid, forceful experiences of direct sensation or feeling, and 'ideas,' the fainter copies or images of those impressions that occur in thinking and remembering. Complex ideas (like a 'winged horse') can combine simple ideas in new ways, but every simple idea must ultimately trace back to a corresponding simple impression.
precise_definition: Hume's foundational distinction: impressions 'have more force and violence,' while 'by ideas I mean the faint images of these in thinking and reasoning'; his key principle is that 'every simple idea has a simple impression, which resembles it; and every simple impression a correspondent idea,' with complex ideas (which need not resemble any single impression) built out of simple ones.
why_it_mattered: This distinction is the foundation of Hume's entire epistemology and his most famous methodological maxim -- 'no idea without an antecedent impression' -- inherited from Locke but stated with far greater rigor and consistency.
historical_origin: Opens Book I of the Treatise of Human Nature (1739).
examples: A man born blind has no idea of colours, since he has never had the corresponding impressions
We can imagine a winged horse (a complex idea) despite never perceiving one, because its components (wings, horse) are each drawn from real impressions
objections: Russell's psychological objection: Hume ignores vagueness -- a recalled image of a specific shade of colour or a specific height is rarely precise enough to distinguish it from very similar shades or heights, contrary to Hume's claim that ideas 'exactly represent' their impressions
This vagueness explains, contra Hume's own difficulty, how we might imagine an intermediate shade of colour between two similar shades we have actually seen
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became the central axiom of the entire empiricist tradition following Hume.
